claims.text: Near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles can be encapsulated by several graphene layers.
The starting nanoparticles are compositionally uniform solid solutions.
Graphene-shell encapsulation provides extrinsic stabilization to near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles.
Graphene-shell encapsulation curbs atomic diffusion within or at the surface of the nanoparticles.
Graphene-shell encapsulation suppresses elemental surface segregation.
Graphene-shell encapsulation preserves nanoparticle structural and chemical integrity under high-temperature catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
The graphene shell acts as a physical barrier that limits surface-atom mobility.
The graphene shell prevents nanoparticle agglomeration.
The graphene shell reduces nanoparticle exposure to reactive species that can drive segregation.
High-entropy stabilization can reduce atomic diffusion through high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, preserving a uniform elemental distribution during annealing.
Graphene encapsulation enhances the alloy's intrinsic high-entropy stabilization.
Relative to unencapsulated controls, graphene-encapsulated nanoparticles will undergo less coarsening under high thermal loads.
Relative to unencapsulated controls, graphene-encapsulated nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation under high thermal loads.
Relative to unencapsulated controls, graphene-encapsulated nanoparticles will undergo fewer phase transformations under high thermal loads.
The stabilization effect depends on the graphene shell remaining structurally intact.
The stabilization effect is expected only for nanoparticle systems synthesized with homogeneous compositions.
The magnitude of stabilization and the optimal graphene thickness may vary with alloy composition and reactive environment.
Varying graphene-shell presence and thickness while holding particle composition, size, synthesis history, and thermal exposure constant can isolate the effect of encapsulation.
